Evidence Readings / When the unit changes, the story changes
Evidence Reading

Are we counting people, accounts, active accounts, subscribers, wallets, terminals or transactions?

When the unit changes, the story changes

People, accounts, subscribers, terminals and transactions all describe parts of Yemen’s financial system. They are not interchangeable measures of financial inclusion, and a target or a trend is only as sound as the unit it keeps.

Evidence periodGlobal Findex fieldwork 2022–2023 · point-of-sale (POS) counts March 2025 – June 2026 · project baseline January 2025, target 2030
Last reviewed3 October 2026

What not to conclude

Accounts, active accounts, subscribers, wallets, terminals and transactions cannot be converted into unique people, and a target cannot be compared with a result whose unit, population or activity definition differs.

01Start with the noun02The denominator still matters03Programme measures are legitimate within their own universe04When targets drift05What would change this reading?06Trace the evidence07Sources08Related measurement priorities09Related readings

Financial-inclusion figures can all move in the same direction and still tell us different things. Adults with an account, accounts on a provider’s books, registered wallet subscribers, active accounts, transactions, POS terminals, programme beneficiaries: each can be useful. The problem begins when one quietly takes the place of another.

Yemen’s representative Findex evidence measures people. Administrative systems count accounts and other financial products, infrastructure and activity. Programmes count the firms or beneficiaries they support. These measures can describe one financial system without measuring one outcome.

Start with the noun

“11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed had an account” (Global Findex, fieldwork 2022–2023) and “POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden rose from 561 to 1,651 between March 2025 and June 2026, within its reporting scope” are both legitimate observations. The first is about people, estimated from a weighted survey. The second is about pieces of infrastructure counted in an administrative system.

One terminal can serve many people, and one person can use many terminals. A person can hold several accounts; an account can generate many transactions; a registered subscriber may be inactive.

The noun is part of the metric. Change the noun and the story can change without anything changing in reality.

The denominator still matters

Even when the counted object is people, the denominator cannot disappear. The Yemen Findex study has 1,000 respondents, but population estimates require the survey weights and design. The respondents are the observations from which the estimate is made, not the denominator of Yemen’s adult population, and raw case percentages are not population estimates. The survey frame also excludes areas holding about 23% of the population.

Programme measures are legitimate within their own universe

The World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project sets a 2030 target of 1,021 access points against a January 2025 baseline of 817, under the project’s own definition. That is legitimate project-monitoring evidence.

It is not a count of people. Nor can it be added to, or compared directly with, counts of ATMs, POS terminals or agents unless the project’s access-point definitions and de-duplication rules are documented, and in the evidence base they are not. A bounded measure is not weak because its universe is narrow; it becomes misleading when that universe disappears from view.

When targets drift

A baseline may measure adults with an account. Monitoring may later report registered accounts; a dashboard may highlight active wallets; a performance report may celebrate transactions; and the final narrative may call the result greater inclusion. Every number in that chain can be correct while the chain itself is wrong. That is metric drift.

Before accepting any baseline, target or claim of progress, ask:

  • What exactly is being counted?
  • Among whom does the number apply?
  • What makes the unit active, or included?
  • Are the baseline and the result measured under the same definition?
  • What does the measure still not tell us?

What would change this reading?

A metric crosswalk for Yemen’s main inclusion measures, recording for each one what is counted, whether units are unique, the universe, the denominator, the activity rule, the period, the source, any link to unique people or firms, and whether it measures access, registration, active use, frequency, quality or outcome. Where a bridge is missing, the gap should be visible rather than filled by assumption.

The practical rule:

Do not compare two numbers until you can complete this sentence for both: “This counts ___ among ___ under the rule ___ during ___.”

If the blanks differ materially, the first question is not how much the number changed. It is whether there is a comparison at all.

Related measurement priorities

Each priority below would supply evidence that this Reading says is missing; the link does not mean the priority would settle the Reading.

Measurement priorityP0 · Providers / Geography
A register of active financial access points
Current official rosters establish selected listing, licensing and event states, but do not provide a complete, geocoded register of active branches, agents, merchants and other service points.
Evidence needed: An authoritative or jointly documented register of individual access points recording type, active status, date, location and services, plus population denominators and road-network data that allow coverage and travel distance or time to be calculated.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish listing and licensing from operation and observed access before any access or opportunity map is interpreted.
Open this measurement priority
Measurement priorityP0 · Payments / People
Active and repeat digital use
Administrative data show registrations, infrastructure and transactions, while historical evidence also records dormancy and one-time or imposed use; unique repeat users are not measured consistently.
Evidence needed: Administrative data from providers or payment systems, with deduplication rules, and/or demand-side active-use measures.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish registration or temporary activity from repeat use, merchant use and sustained financial use.
Open this measurement priority

Related readings

Evidence periodProvider data 2016–2019, from a 2020 study of five e-money providers
When does digital growth become durable use?
Historical evidence from Yemen records a large base of e-money accounts by 2019 alongside dormancy, one-off use and a transaction mix still closely tied to cash. The open question is whether people choose to return to digital finance and find enough value to keep using it.
Evidence periodWorld Bank Yemen Enterprise Survey, September 2022, seven governorates · SMEPS programme report for 2024
How can 22% and 91.84% both be right?
A 2022 survey of formal firms in seven selected governorates can tell us that finance was named less often than electricity or fuel, and also that most firms in a narrower group rated finance a major or moderate obstacle. The numbers do not contradict each other. They answer different questions.
